reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: Disorder of leucine catabolism caused by biallelic variants in MCCC1 or MCCC2 encoding the two subunits of the enzyme
One of the most frequently detected conditions on expanded newborn screening, yet most identified individuals remain asymptomatic
When symptomatic, presents with episodes of metabolic acidosis, hypoglycaemia, hyperammonaemia, vomiting and lethargy, often during catabolic illness
Characteristic acylcarnitine finding is elevated 3-hydroxyisovalerylcarnitine (C5-OH), which flags it on screening
Urine organic acids show raised 3-methylcrotonylglycine and 3-hydroxyisovalerate
A low free carnitine state is common and may be the presenting biochemical abnormality
Maternal 3-MCC deficiency can be unmasked by an abnormal newborn screen in an unaffected infant
Management is often just avoidance of prolonged fasting and carnitine supplementation, with mild leucine restriction and an emergency regimen in symptomatic cases
reference.pathophysiology: 3-Methylcrotonyl-CoA carboxylase is a biotin-dependent mitochondrial enzyme that catalyses a step in the degradation of leucine, converting 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA to 3-methylglutaconyl-CoA. Deficiency, from defects in either the alpha (MCCC1) or beta (MCCC2) subunit, blocks leucine catabolism so that 3-methylcrotonyl-CoA is diverted to 3-methylcrotonylglycine and 3-hydroxyisovaleric acid, which accumulate and are excreted. The conjugation of these metabolites with carnitine and glycine can deplete free carnitine. Although the biochemical defect is consistent, clinical expression is highly variable and often benign, so it is regarded as a condition of low and unpredictable penetrance. During catabolic stress a minority develop a Reye-like metabolic crisis with acidosis and hyperammonaemia. Inheritance is autosomal recessive.
additionalDifferentials: Holocarboxylase synthetase or biotinidase deficiency (multiple carboxylase defects)
Primary carnitine transporter deficiency (for low free carnitine)
Fatty acid oxidation disorders presenting with hypoketotic hypoglycaemia
Maternal 3-MCC deficiency detected through the infant's screen
additionalInvestigations: Plasma acylcarnitine profile showing elevated C5-OH (3-hydroxyisovalerylcarnitine)
Plasma free and total carnitine levels
Blood gas, glucose and ammonia during suspected crises
MCCC1 and MCCC2 gene sequencing for confirmation
Enzyme activity assay in fibroblasts/leukocytes where needed
Maternal biochemical testing when a newborn screen is abnormal but the infant is well
redFlags: Metabolic acidosis with hyperammonaemia and encephalopathy during illness
Hypoglycaemia with lethargy in a catabolic child
Severe carnitine depletion with hypotonia or cardiac concern
Reye-like deterioration during intercurrent infection or fasting
reference.prognosis: The great majority of individuals identified are asymptomatic with a normal outlook; a minority experience metabolic crises, and with fasting avoidance and carnitine supplementation the prognosis is generally good.
pitfalls: Over-treating or over-restricting asymptomatic screen-positive infants given the low penetrance
Failing to consider maternal 3-MCC deficiency when a healthy infant screens positive
Missing symptomatic decompensation by assuming the condition is always benign
Allowing prolonged perioperative or illness-related fasting without an emergency plan
references: Scriver's Online Metabolic and Molecular Bases of Inherited Disease (OMMBID)
